hook.line: Tomás is writing to the city office about the cooperative, and the last line of the email needs an "in advance". Spanish has two, and they are not interchangeable: one is for thanking and knowing, the other for leaving yourself time.

examples.es: Les agradezco de antemano su respuesta.
examples.en: I thank you all in advance for your reply. (formal)
You have to pay in advance.
Please let me know in advance. (formal)

rule:
English uses "in advance" for everything. Spanish splits it in two.

*de antemano*: before something happens, you already feel it, know it or say it. Thanking, knowing, apologising, expecting: *gracias de antemano*, *lo sabía de antemano*.

*con antelación*: you act early and leave real time before a date. Booking, paying, warning, arriving: *reservar con antelación*, *avisar con antelación*.

A quick test: if you are leaving a margin before a deadline, it is *con antelación*. If it is a thought or a feeling that comes before the event, it is *de antemano*. In everyday speech *con anticipación* is a common twin of *con antelación*.
smallPrint: Both are adverbial phrases. *De antemano* is also a standing phrase in formal letters; *con antelación* is the standard one for notices and bookings.

options: Thanks in advance, before you've even done it.
You have to pay in advance.
You have to thank people beforehand.

readAndPick.es: Les agradezco de antemano su respuesta.
options: I'll reply to you all with time to spare. (formal)
I thank you all in advance for your reply. (formal)
Please let me know in advance. (formal)

readAndPick.es: Sé de antemano que va a decir que no.
options: I already know he'll say no.
I'll leave time in case he says no.

readAndPick.es: Dígame con antelación si no puede venir.
options: Tell me ahead of time if you can't come. (formal)
Tell me afterwards if you can't come. (formal)

readAndPick.es: Pagamos con antelación para tener la sala.
options: We paid after getting the room.
We paid ahead of time to get the room.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *de antemano* or *con antelación* and type the whole sentence: Gracias ___.
yourTurn.why: Thanking is a feeling that comes before the event: *de antemano*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *de antemano* or *con antelación* and type the whole sentence: Hay que reservar ___.
yourTurn.why: Booking leaves time before a date: *con antelación*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say (formal, to one person): Please let me know in advance.
yourTurn.why: A warning only helps if it comes early, so *con antelación*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say (formal, to several people): I thank you in advance for your reply.
yourTurn.answer: Les agradezco de antemano su respuesta.
accept: Les agradezco de antemano la respuesta.
yourTurn.why: Thanks before the reply is *de antemano*, and *les* is for several people.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: You have to pay in advance.
yourTurn.why: Paying early is leaving a margin: *con antelación*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it formal, to one person: *Gracias de antemano por la respuesta.*
yourTurn.answer: Le agradezco de antemano la respuesta.
accept: Le agradezco de antemano su respuesta.
yourTurn.why: *Le agradezco* is the formal "I thank you", and *de antemano* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it past: *Sé de antemano que va a decir que no.* (I knew beforehand that he would say no.)
yourTurn.answer: Sabía de antemano que iba a decir que no.
yourTurn.why: Knowing beforehand is still *de antemano*; only the verbs move to the past.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Thanks is not a booking; for thanking before the event Spanish uses *de antemano*.
Almost. *En avance* is a copy of the English; the Spanish phrase is *de antemano*.
Almost. Knowing is not leaving time before a deadline, so *de antemano*.

personal: Think of something you booked or paid for early, and something you knew was going to happen. Say both, one with *con antelación* and one with *de antemano*.
